passage: Thomas had eleven minutes before his counsellor's appointment, and the auto was stuck behind a wedding procession. His phone buzzed: a reply from the hostel warden, three lines, nothing about the seniors who had hurt him two years ago or the complaints he had made. His thumb hovered over the screen. He typed, I hope you lose your job, then held down delete. Beside him sat Chinmay, a friend from the hostel, who said, "Say what you actually want." Thomas breathed out. "I want them to admit it. I want the college to have a proper committee." He drafted a short email asking for a written response and a meeting with the principal, and saved it for the counsellor to read before sending. The procession finally moved.

qa.q: How many minutes did Thomas have before his counsellor's appointment?
What did Thomas really want when he deleted his angry line?
qa.a: He wanted the harm to be admitted and the college to set up a proper committee, not revenge on the warden, so he deleted the angry line.

qa.q: How did Thomas turn his anger into something useful?
qa.a: He drafted a short email asking for a written response and a meeting with the principal, and saved it for the counsellor to read before sending.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see Thomas's first typed message?
qa.a: Chinmay probably understands the fury but nudges Thomas with "Say what you actually want", hinting that the angry line would not bring Thomas what he needs.

grounding: Thomas's anger at those who harmed him and failed to protect him is channelled into a written request and a meeting through proper channels instead of revenge, despite time pressure.

passage:
Anirban's diary. Tuesday.

Four months since the road-rage attack, and today I saw the man again. Same red car, same market. I stood there shaking with rage. I wanted to smash his windscreen. I'm not proud of it.

The police still haven't filed the chargesheet. The shopkeeper who saw everything told me to "move on." Move on? He broke my nose.

I rang Reena instead of doing anything stupid. She's been my friend since school. She let me shout for ten minutes. Then she said, "Your anger is right. But smashing his car puts you in the lockup, not him."

She's right. So tonight I wrote down every date: the attack, the hospital, each visit to the police station. Tomorrow I'll go with her to the legal aid clinic and ask how to push the case. I'll also ask the counsellor there for help with the anger, because I can't carry this alone.

I also changed my route to work. That's not fear. That's a boundary.

qa.q: What did the man who attacked Anirban drive?
What was Anirban feeling when he saw the man again?
qa.a: Anirban felt enraged and shaken, wanting to smash the man's windscreen.

qa.q: How is Anirban channelling the anger, and why is it wise?
qa.a: By writing down dates, going to legal aid to push the case, seeing a counsellor and changing route, which seeks justice and safety instead of revenge.

qa.q: How does Reena see Anirban's anger?
qa.a: Reena sees it as justified but wants Anirban to channel it properly so it doesn't land Anirban in trouble.

grounding: The diary shows someone angry at a person who harmed them and at slow police, choosing boundaries and justice through legal aid and counselling instead of revenge.

passage:
Rashmi: I found his address
Rashmi: the guy who kept following me after college. the college did nothing when I complained
Rashmi: I want to post it everywhere. let people see who he is
Kalyani: I'm so sorry. You have every right to be angry
Kalyani: the college failing you makes me angry too
Rashmi: so you agree
Kalyani: I agree you should be safe and he should face consequences
Kalyani: but if you post his address, it could backfire on you. legally too
Rashmi: so I just do nothing? again?
Kalyani: no. not nothing
Kalyani: file a police complaint for stalking. I'll come with you tomorrow
Kalyani: my cousin at the legal aid centre can tell you about protection options
Kalyani: and the women's helpline has counsellors, for the anger too
Rashmi: I'm so tired of being the one who has to be careful
Kalyani: I know. it's not fair. but you deserve justice that sticks
Rashmi: ok. tomorrow morning. police station
Kalyani: I'll be at yours at 9

qa.a: The address of the man who kept following Rashmi after college.

qa.q: What was Rashmi feeling while wanting to post the address?
qa.a: Rashmi felt furious and exhausted, let down by the college and tired of being the one who has to be careful.

qa.q: What did Kalyani suggest instead of posting the address, and why?
qa.a: A police complaint for stalking, legal aid for protection options and the helpline for the anger, because proper channels bring lasting safety and justice without backfiring.

qa.q: How does Kalyani see Rashmi's anger?
qa.a: Kalyani sees it as valid and shares it, but wants to help Rashmi use it safely.

grounding: The chat shows someone angry at a stalker and a college that failed to protect them, and a friend helping channel that anger into police, legal aid and support rather than revenge.
